posts.name: Donner
posts.cooked:
In computer programming, this would be:

Monolithic design vs. object oriented design.

In monolithic, everything is in one big block.  You only have to copy one file over, but searching for anything can be long and tedious.  Maintaining monolithic code is a lot harder.

In object oriented design, you have a separate file for each "object" (usually a section of code representing some aspect of the program that may be accessed from multiple different locations in the main code or that may have multiple instances of itself created, like building blocks).  Finding a bug in an object just means checking through that object's code.  You have a lot more files to keep track of so file names are very important, but maintenance is much easier.

In every case I have seen, the object oriented design was much better overall than the monolithic approach.  In this case, I have to agree with Silverleaf.  It makes it much easier to search for the relevant thread this way.  We may get more threads overall, but getting to the one we want when we want it becomes much easier.

Silverleaf:

Ease of future searching, as I've explained before. And how is it "grotesquely wasteful"? It's not like it's written on paper or anything.

Thread proliferation.  Takes up space on the feed.  Fewer threads are better.  Search is worthless anyway, so "ease of future searching" is a lost cause IMO.  Really, we need a rulings index.

So last week I experienced a particular situation where I wanted to check what the ruling was. I knew it had come up recently because I remembered reading it only a little while before, but I didn't know which thread it was in.

That happens to me a lot too, but because I don't have a portable computer, usually I just have to make a spot ruling and get on with the game.

Seperate threads with sensible, descriptive titles means we don't waste time searching

But unless you remember the EXACT wording of the thread title, how are you going to find it?  If you tried to find this thread by searching "cards under Promo Blade" (prior to my typing that exact phrase in this post, of course, and possibly even thereafter since the search seems to be ANY-based rather than ALL-based), you'd probably find five thousand other threads but NOT this one.  Your best hope to find this thread would be to search ONLY the word "facing".  If you didn't happen to remember that this exact, fairly unusual word was in the title (which you likely wouldn't, since it's not really the most pertinent part of what the topic is about; you'd think of "Blade" or "Promo" much sooner I think, or even "face up or face down", which wouldn't work at all because it'd find every topic containing the word "or"), you'd have very little hope of finding the right thread, and even less of finding it promptly.

But, if it was under a SINGLE "all rules questions go here" thread, whose topic creator (or a moderator) regularly went through and indexed it, you'd be fine.  We have something pretty close to that already with the Spiffworld ratings collective, though he insists on keeping that in a PDF rather than a Web-browsable text file (I know web browsers can sometimes open or "preview" PDFs now, but it's the sort of thing that can easily be impaired by all manner of technical issues), and he refuses to include rulings that are generally agreed upon by the community unless they've been confirmed by the >G crew.

because it's immediately obvious which one we want.If you take your opinion to extremes, we'd just have one thread with everything in it and no one would be able to find anything.

As opposed to ten thousand threads with everything in them and no one can find anything?  What I proposed was much more of a compromise solution.

posts.cooked:
I'm actually talking about the "scanning the list of thread titles" type of searching. If I'm looking for something about the order that Friction plays cards in, I'll pick up this thread very quickly now it has a title that references that. I couldn't do that before with the original, hugely unhelpful title.

Sure, the search on here isn't great. But that isn't an excuse to use bad thread titles, because the forum search isn't the only way people find things. It's also helpful for those people who might want to choose which threads to read (rather than reading every single thing like I tend to do), because it's much more difficult than it needs to be to assess which ones are relevant to you if they have generic titles. If everything's called "I have a few questions" then you can't even remember which was the one about the Chairman's flip side and which one was about whether you can discard your hand if you don't have any cards in it. 

I agree that some kind of index would be great. But we don't have one, and so letting questions get buried in a composite monster thread is hardly ideal. More threads are much better, especially as comments in a composite thread would get mixed up with each other chronologically so if you were only interested in one question you'd have to sift through replies to other questions to find what you needed. More than likely a new person faced with this will just create a new thread to redundantly ask their question that has already been thoroughly answered and discussed elsewhere, which basically wastes everyone's time.

posts.name: Edwin
posts.cooked:
Silverleaf:

I'm actually talking about the "scanning the list of thread titles" type of searching.

But how many do you want to scan?  If the thread I'm looking for isn't on the New Topics or Active Topics or maaaaybe page 1 of Rules and Gameplay, I lack the patience to keep looking.  But if it's a thread I created for rules questions I myself asked, I can always find it in my Created Topics.  It'd be even better if there was a Subscribed Topics function, of course, so I could find threads others have created.  But the more different threads there are, the fewer of them fit in one list, so the more lists you have to look through to find them, and I'm not going to sit around going through page after page of lists trying to find something.

More than likely a new person faced with this will just create a new thread to redundantly ask their question that has already been thoroughly answered and discussed elsewhere, which basically wastes everyone's time.

That much we agree on at least.  But that's not really a solvable problem, not unless >G will write a real rulebook for the game, instead of the splashy comic-font large-print "Look How Awesome Our Game Is" intro book that hardly tells you anything about how to actually play (though of course the bio information is nice).  As long as the game's default position on how to solve rules conundrum is "uh, what do YOU think is right; it's you're game, so do whatever you think is fun", those threads are going to get created.

Just today in my ERT class, we looked at a rather simplistic psychological model which postulated four basic types of people, and one of the analyses it used was about each one's most fundamental need.  One of the four types was listed as "Needs to be correct," and people like that just aren't completely happy playing a game with such an imprecise rulebook, no matter how awesome the game is overall.  They - or perhaps I should say "we" - can't just accept "decide for yourself" as an answer; we need to have the RIGHT answer.
